transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I came in because I barely sleep right anymore. I'll just lie there at night, hearing the rain or... thinking about the bluff giving way. And then when I finally do pass out, I wake up all sweaty from these dreams. I end up showing up to my shift at the call center feeling like I never even slept.
Have you experienced or witnessed an event involving actual or threatened death or serious injury?
Yeah. I mean... just what I mentioned a minute ago about the bluff giving way. I guess that would count as threatened death or serious injury. I'm not really sure what else to call it, but... yeah.
Did a bluff actually give way or otherwise place you in immediate danger, or is this something you fear might happen?
No, it actually happened. It's not just something I'm worried about... the ground actually gave out while I was right there. So, yeah, it was a real thing that happened.
How long ago did the bluff give way?
It's been about four months. That's when I got trapped after the trail collapsed on the bluff. Everything with the sleep and the dreams has just been going on ever since then.
Since the bluff collapse, have you been avoiding places that remind you of what happened?

Yeah, definitely. I won't go anywhere near the coast trails now. I just... I can't do it. And I've even been dodging texts from my hiking buddies. Just the thought of talking about going back out there makes my chest tighten up. So I just avoid it all.
Do your nightmares replay the bluff collapse, or are they about something else?

Yeah, they are about the bluff. That's actually why I came in, because I just barely sleep right anymore. I'll lie there at night, hearing the rain or... just thinking about the bluff giving way. And then when I finally do pass out, I wake up all sweaty from those dreams. Then I have to show up to my shift at the call center feeling like I never even slept.
Since the bluff collapse, have unwanted memories or images of it suddenly come to you while you are awake?

Yeah, that happens a lot. Stuff just pops into my head out of nowhere. Like, I'll suddenly hear the sound of the rocks sliding, or I'll feel like my leg is stuck under me again. It's really weird because for a minute, it feels like I'm right back on that trail, even though I'm just sitting at my desk with my headset on at work. It just hits me when I'm not even thinking about it.
Since the bluff collapse, have you felt unusually on guard or watchful, as if danger could happen at any moment?

No, I haven't really noticed feeling like that. I mean, I don't feel like I'm constantly looking over my shoulder or expecting something bad to happen out of nowhere. It's more just the memories and the dreams that are messing with me. But as far as feeling on edge all the time... no, not really.
Since the bluff collapse, have you been unusually irritable or had angry outbursts?

Yeah, actually. Um, especially at work. My patience is just... way shorter than it used to be. I've snapped at a few customers over really small stuff on the phone. I even raised my voice enough the other day that my supervisor had to pull me aside and talk to me about it. I just get frustrated a lot faster now.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient experienced an actual life-threatening bluff collapse four months ago, followed by recurrent distressing memories, trauma-related nightmares, flashback-like experiences, avoidance of reminders, irritability, sleep disturbance, and occupational impairment. Symptoms have persisted beyond one month, supporting post-traumatic stress disorder rather than acute stress disorder.

Flashback-like experiences of hearing rocks slide and feeling trapped as though the event were happening again.
Avoids coastal trails and other places associated with the collapse.
Avoids texts and discussions with hiking companions related to returning to the area.
Increased irritability and angry outbursts, including snapping at customers and raising their voice at work.
Marked sleep disturbance with difficulty sleeping and nonrestorative sleep.
